entries.title: Your Redstone Guide
pages:
§6CRAFT YOUR BOOK§r
Combine 1 redstone dust and 1 leather in any two crafting slots. Their order and position do not matter. The result is one reusable guide.

§6READ IT§r
Hold the guide in your main hand and use Read Guide. On a computer, right-click. Aim away from chests and other interactive blocks.

§6FIND A TOPIC§r
Components explains how each part works. Recipes shows exact crafting rows. Three Builds gives step-by-step projects. Resume Reading remembers your last page for this player in this world.

The guide uses Minecraft's touch-friendly reading menus, not the vanilla written-book screen. The in-game item now uses the selected closed-book icon.

entries.title: Power, distance, and ticks
pages:
§6SIGNAL STRENGTH§r
Redstone strength ranges from 0 (off) to 15. Dust loses one level with each step along a line, so a full-strength source reaches up to 15 dust positions. Put a repeater before the signal runs out to start a fresh full-strength line.

§6PULSES AND DELAYS§r
A lever stays on. A button gives a temporary signal. One redstone tick is 2 game ticks, normally 0.1 second; lag can make real time longer. A repeater adds 1-4 redstone ticks of delay.

§6DIRECTIONS MATTER§r
Repeater and comparator arrows point toward their output. An observer watches with its face and outputs through its red-dot side. Test each part with a lever and lamp before adding the next part.

entries.title: Bedrock rules that matter
pages:
§6USE BEDROCK DESIGNS§r
Java tutorials are not always transferable. Bedrock pistons, droppers, and dispensers do not use Java's quasi-connectivity. Give them a direct, ordinary power path.

§6PISTONS§r
Do not rely on Java one-tick sticky-piston block-spitting. Bedrock can move many container blocks, but immovable blocks and the 12-block push limit still matter.

§6OBSERVERS§r
The exact updates detected can differ between editions. Check a sensor with a lamp before wiring a full farm.

§6SIMULATION§r
Circuits and crop growth depend on the area being simulated. This guide does not keep chunks loaded. Test at your world's normal simulation distance.

Make a copy of a valuable world before testing any new add-on.

entries.title: Why is my circuit not working?
pages:
§6CHECK IN THIS ORDER§r
1. Is there actually a power source? Follow the lit dust from the source to the output.
2. Is the dust line too long? Insert a repeater while the incoming signal is still positive.
3. Are repeaters, comparators, observers, hoppers, and pistons facing the right way?
4. Is a hopper accidentally powered and locked?
5. Is a piston blocked by an immovable block or more than 12 blocks?
6. Does your machine need repeated pulses rather than constant power? Dispensers, droppers, and crafters act on new activations.
7. Is this a Java-only tutorial?

§6BOOK HELP§r
Missing icon: activate this add-on's Resource pack. No reading menu: activate its Behavior pack, close other screens, and reopen the world. This book does not need an internet connection.

entries.title: Redstone dust
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Carries a signal over supported surfaces. Each step reduces the strength by one. Adjacent wires can connect and accidentally join two circuits.

§6COMMON USES§r
Connect switches to doors and lamps; distribute a signal; make timing and logic circuits.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Build lever > dust > repeater > lamp. Leave a gap between circuits you want to keep separate.

entries.title: Redstone torch
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Normally supplies power. It switches off when the block it is attached to is powered, so it can invert an input: on becomes off.

§6COMMON USES§r
NOT gates, torch towers, simple clocks, and default-on lighting.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Attach a torch to one side of a block and a lever to another. Flip the lever. Extremely rapid switching can temporarily burn a torch out.

entries.title: Block of redstone
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A constant strength-15 power source. It does not turn off like a torch and can be moved by pistons.

§6COMMON USES§r
Movable power sources, compact permanent power, and storing nine redstone dust.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Keep it away from hoppers you want running: powering a hopper locks its own transfer mechanism.

entries.title: Redstone repeater
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Accepts power at its rear and sends strength 15 out its front. Use it to select 1, 2, 3, or 4 redstone ticks of delay.

§6COMMON USES§r
Extend long wires; isolate one direction; synchronize piston and lamp circuits.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A powered repeater or comparator pointing into its side can lock its current output. Dust alone does not provide that side-locking input.

entries.title: Redstone comparator
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Reads its rear input and the stronger side input. Compare mode passes the rear strength only when it is at least the side strength. Subtract mode outputs rear minus side, with a minimum of zero.

§6COMMON USES§r
Read container fullness, filter items, make threshold detectors, and process analog signals.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Use the comparator to toggle modes; the small front torch lights in subtract mode. Its output points away from the container being read.

entries.title: Comparator readings
pages:
§6READING CONTAINERS§r
An empty ordinary inventory reads 0. Nonempty inventories produce 1-15 according to the average fraction filled across all slots. Fullness is not simply the number of items: stack sizes matter.

§6SPECIAL READINGS§r
Lectern: page position.
Chiseled bookshelf: last slot interacted with, not number of books.
Cake: remaining slices.
Cauldron: fill state.
Composter: composting level.
Item frame: rotation of an inserted item.
Copper bulb: lit state.
Crafter: occupied plus disabled slots.
Copper golem statue: pose.

§6BUILD A TEST BENCH§r
Place a comparator pointing away from the block, then 15 dust in a straight line. Count lit positions. Use a full solid block behind an item frame to read it.

entries.title: Solid blocks as conductors
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Many full opaque blocks can carry power. A repeater pointing into a block strongly powers it, allowing dust on the far side to take a signal. Glass does not behave like this.

§6COMMON USES§r
Hide wiring in walls, pass a signal through a block, and distribute power to adjacent mechanisms.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Put a repeater into stone and a lamp beside that stone. Do not assume slabs, glass, or decorative blocks conduct like a full stone block.

entries.title: Lever
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A manual on/off switch that stays in its chosen state until used again.

§6COMMON USES§r
Master switches, testing circuits, hopper locks, and toggled doors.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Start a new circuit with a lever before replacing it with an automatic sensor.

entries.title: Wooden buttons
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Give a temporary signal when pressed. Wooden variants normally stay on for 1.5 seconds and can also be held active by a lodged arrow.

§6COMMON USES§r
Door openers, target puzzles, and manual pulses for dispensers.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A wooden button offers more walking time through a door than a stone button. All wood species serve the same redstone role.

entries.title: Stone button
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Produces a short strength-15 signal when a player presses it, normally lasting one second. Unlike a wooden button, it is not activated by arrows.

§6COMMON USES§r
Compact door controls, dependable player-triggered pulses, and testing.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Put a button on the solid block beside the lower half of an iron door.

entries.title: Polished blackstone button
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Acts like a stone button: a player-triggered temporary signal, normally one second long. Its material changes the appearance, not its basic logic.

§6COMMON USES§r
Dark-themed door controls and Nether builds.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Use polished blackstone, not ordinary blackstone, in its recipe.

entries.title: Wooden pressure plates
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Produce power when an entity rests on them, including players, mobs, and dropped items.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic doors, item detection, and entrance triggers.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A dropped item can keep one on. Use a stone plate when you only want living entities to trigger it.

entries.title: Stone pressure plate
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Activates for players and mobs standing on it; dropped items do not activate it.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic entrances and mob-triggered circuits.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
It is not player-only. Mobs can use a plate-controlled entrance too.

entries.title: Polished blackstone pressure plate
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Functions like a stone pressure plate and detects players and mobs, not dropped items.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic doors in dark builds and mob triggers.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Keep surrounding redstone isolated so the plate does not power a second door accidentally.

entries.title: Light weighted pressure plate
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A gold plate with variable output. Its signal grows with the number of entities resting on it, up to strength 15.

§6COMMON USES§r
Analog entity detection and measuring groups rather than just on/off presence.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A dropped stack is an item entity; do not assume the displayed item count equals the plate's entity count.

entries.title: Heavy weighted pressure plate
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
An iron plate whose output increases more slowly than the gold version, in groups of ten entities, up to strength 15.

§6COMMON USES§r
Detect large groups of entities and build analog thresholds.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Use a comparator or a measured dust line when you need a threshold rather than any nonzero signal.

entries.title: Tripwire hook
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Two hooks attached to facing solid surfaces become a detector when a continuous straight line of tripwire connects them.

§6COMMON USES§r
Hallway alarms, mob detectors, and hidden triggers.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Both hooks must face one another at the same height. An unattached hook is not a working detector.

entries.title: Tripwire / placed string
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Placed string links two facing tripwire hooks. An entity touching the connected line activates the hooks.

§6COMMON USES§r
Wide doorway detection and subtle alarms.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Use shears when removing tripwire to avoid the normal breaking trigger. The hook is crafted; string is normally obtained as loot.

entries.title: Target block
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A projectile hit produces a pulse. Hits nearer the center create a stronger signal.

§6COMMON USES§r
Archery games, combination challenges, and projectile-activated doors.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Read it with a comparator or a dust line to distinguish a bullseye from an edge hit.

entries.title: Trapped chest
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Emits redstone power while players have it open, with strength increasing with the number of viewers. It also works as a normal storage inventory.

§6COMMON USES§r
Chest-opening alarms and locking a nearby hopper while a player accesses the chest.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
The opening signal is not the same thing as a comparator reading of inventory fullness.

entries.title: Observer
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Watches the block directly in front of its face. A detected update creates a short full-strength pulse at the red-dot side on the opposite end.

§6COMMON USES§r
Sugar cane farms, block-change detection, and update-triggered machinery.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
The face watches; the red dot outputs. Bedrock does not detect every update in exactly the same way as Java.

entries.title: Daylight detector
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Generates a variable signal affected by daylight, the sky, time, and weather. Use it to switch between normal and inverted modes.

§6COMMON USES§r
Night lighting, day/night indicators, and timed outdoor circuits.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Use inverted mode for night lights and keep the detector exposed to the sky. Weather can change when the lights switch.

entries.title: Sculk sensor
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Detects nearby vibrations from actions such as walking and block interactions, then produces a redstone response.

§6COMMON USES§r
Wireless-feeling alarms, sound-triggered entrances, and activity detection.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Wool blocks vibration paths. Waterlogging removes its audible activation sound, not its ability to detect vibrations. It is obtained with Silk Touch, not crafted.

entries.title: Calibrated sculk sensor
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Uses a redstone input on its amethyst-marked side to filter for a particular vibration frequency. With no filtering input it can listen more generally.

§6COMMON USES§r
More selective vibration triggers and separating different kinds of player actions.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
The calibration strength selects a vibration type; it is not a simple volume setting. Keep unwanted vibration paths blocked with wool.

entries.title: Lightning rod
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Attracts nearby lightning strikes within its effective range and gives a redstone pulse when struck.

§6COMMON USES§r
Storm alarms and lightning-triggered mechanisms.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Do not rely on thunderstorms for an everyday door switch. Keep exposed lightning devices away from flammable structures.

entries.title: Piston
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Extends one block when powered and can push a line of up to 12 movable blocks. An ordinary piston does not pull a block back.

§6COMMON USES§r
Crop harvesting, moving walls, block pushers, and simple doors.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Obsidian and other immovable blocks stop movement. In Bedrock, supply an ordinary direct power path.

entries.title: Sticky piston
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Pushes like a piston, then normally pulls the attached movable block back as it retracts.

§6COMMON USES§r
Retracting doors, bridges, movable redstone blocks, and slime or honey mechanisms.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Do not copy Java-only one-tick block-spitting circuits. The recipe is just a slimeball above a piston.

entries.title: Slime block
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
When moved by a piston, it can carry adjacent blocks that can stick to it. Every moved block still counts toward the push limit.

§6COMMON USES§r
Moving platforms, flying-machine mechanisms, and multi-block doors.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Slime and honey do not stick to each other. Leave clearance so the machine does not grab its surrounding walls.

entries.title: Honey block
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A sticky movement block that can carry adjacent movable blocks in piston mechanisms. It also slows entities touching it.

§6COMMON USES§r
Independent moving sections beside slime blocks, elevators, and moving platforms.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Honey is not a normal redstone conductor. Route power intentionally rather than treating it as stone.

entries.title: Redstone lamp
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Lights while powered, with a brief turn-off delay. It does not remember its state once power is removed.

§6COMMON USES§r
Room lighting, status indicators, and circuit debugging.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Use a copper bulb instead when a brief pulse should toggle the light and leave it in that state.

entries.title: Copper bulb
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Each new redstone activation toggles its light on or off. It remembers the state after the pulse ends. Oxidation reduces brightness.

§6COMMON USES§r
Button-toggle lights, compact memory, and status displays.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Wax preserves oxidation. A comparator reads 15 when the bulb is lit and 0 when unlit. Constant power does not repeatedly toggle it.

entries.title: Note block
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Plays a note on a new redstone activation. Use the block to tune it; the supporting block affects the instrument.

§6COMMON USES§r
Doorbells, musical sequences, and audible status signals.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Leave space above it for an ordinary instrument setup. A repeating clock produces repeated notes; a held lever does not.

entries.title: Bell
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Can ring when activated by redstone and also works as a village gathering bell.

§6COMMON USES§r
Doorbells, alarm indicators, and village-themed notifications.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A single button is enough for a simple bell trigger. Bells are obtained from villages or trading, not a normal crafting recipe.

entries.title: Iron door
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Opens using redstone power instead of ordinary hand interaction. Removing the opening power closes it.

§6COMMON USES§r
Controlled entrances, automatic doors, and secure-looking builds.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Provide an inside control as well as an outside one so players cannot trap themselves.

entries.title: Wooden doors
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Can be opened by hand or by redstone. All wood species serve the same basic redstone role.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic entrances and decorative doors that also have manual access.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A wooden door is not a secure player-only lock. Villagers and some mobs can interact with doors in relevant circumstances.

entries.title: Copper door
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Can be opened by hand and can respond to redstone. Oxidation changes its appearance; waxing preserves the current stage.

§6COMMON USES§r
Redstone-controlled decorative entrances with copper styling.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
It is not an iron door: players can still open it by hand.

entries.title: Iron trapdoor
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Changes between its closed and open orientations when powered. It requires redstone rather than ordinary manual opening.

§6COMMON USES§r
Controlled hatches, gates for entities, and adjustable water-flow barriers.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Check its placement orientation before wiring it; the same power state can look different depending on placement.

entries.title: Wooden trapdoors
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Can be opened by hand or by power. Like other trapdoors, orientation and placement determine the resulting opening.

§6COMMON USES§r
Hatches, mob-farm pathfinding features, and redstone-controlled barriers.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Test the open and closed positions before you put water or entities next to the mechanism.

entries.title: Copper trapdoor
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Works as a manually operable or redstone-controlled hatch, with copper oxidation and waxing for its appearance.

§6COMMON USES§r
Copper-themed hatches, barriers, and controllable decoration.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Oxidation is not a timer for opening the trapdoor. Its open state still follows interaction or power.

entries.title: Fence gate
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Opens by hand or redstone. Removing power closes a redstone-opened gate.

§6COMMON USES§r
Animal enclosures, pathways, and barriers in controlled entrances.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Leave room for the player or mob to pass through the open gate.

entries.title: TNT
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Redstone activation primes TNT, starting a fuse before it explodes and can damage nearby builds.

§6COMMON USES§r
Controlled demolition and minigames in disposable test areas.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Do not test explosives beside your storage or main base. The guide never places or activates TNT automatically.

entries.title: Dispenser
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
On a new power pulse it uses a random occupied slot. Certain items have special actions: firing arrows, dispensing water, or applying bone meal. Other items are ejected.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic watering, bone-meal farms, armor dispensers, and arrow launchers.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
It does not place arbitrary building blocks. A held signal is one activation, not a repeating stream.

entries.title: Dropper
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Moves one item from a random occupied slot on each new activation. It inserts into a suitable container in front or ejects the item into the world.

§6COMMON USES§r
Item elevators, reward dispensers, and controlled transfers.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A dropper ejects a water bucket as an item; a dispenser can use that bucket to place water.

entries.title: Hopper
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Collects loose items above, pulls from a container above, and pushes toward its spout. Redstone power locks its own collection and transfer actions.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic storage, furnace loading, and item sorters.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Sneak-place it against the destination so its spout points correctly. A powered hopper can still receive items pushed into it by another device.

entries.title: Crafter
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Crafts one valid recipe on a new redstone activation and sends its output forward. Disable unused grid slots to help automated ingredient distribution.

§6COMMON USES§r
Turn farm products into blocks, craft supplies automatically, and make production lines.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A comparator reports occupied plus disabled slots, not ordinary inventory fullness. A constant signal does not continuously craft.

entries.title: Chest
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Stores items for hoppers and droppers. A comparator pointing away from it measures inventory fullness.

§6COMMON USES§r
Storage buffers, fullness alarms, and collection points.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
An ordinary chest does not emit opening power like a trapped chest. It needs a comparator for a fullness signal.

entries.title: Barrel
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A storage inventory that hoppers can fill or empty and a comparator can read. It can open even with a solid block above it.

§6COMMON USES§r
Compact storage buffers and circuits with restricted vertical space.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
It can also be a villager workstation. Placement in a village can change which villager claims it.

entries.title: Copper chest
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Provides storage and participates in copper-golem item sorting. Inventory automation and comparator readings are useful for monitoring the stored contents.

§6COMMON USES§r
Input buffers for copper-golem sorting and themed storage systems.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A copper golem is not a redstone wire. Treat its movement and sorting time separately from deterministic redstone timing.

entries.title: Shulker box
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A portable inventory that retains contents when broken. Hoppers transfer its items and a comparator can measure fullness.

§6COMMON USES§r
Bulk storage loading and unloading stations.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Use a dispenser for automated shulker-box placement. Building a reliable full-box breaker requires a tested Bedrock design.

entries.title: Furnace
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Smelts items and has input, fuel, and output slots. Hoppers above load input; side hoppers load fuel; hoppers below remove output. A comparator reads its inventory.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic smelters and detecting whether a smelter contains items.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Redstone does not directly turn smelting on and off; control the ingredient or fuel supply instead.

entries.title: Blast furnace
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Smelts supported metal-related items faster than a normal furnace. Hopper access and inventory comparator readings support automation.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automated ore-processing lines.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
It cannot cook every furnace recipe. Test your ingredient first.

entries.title: Smoker
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Cooks supported food recipes faster than a normal furnace and accepts hopper-based loading and unloading.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic food cooking and farming outputs.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
It is for food, not ore smelting. Control supplies with hoppers rather than expecting power to stop the smoker.

entries.title: Brewing stand
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Brews potions when supplied with suitable bottles, ingredients, and blaze-powder fuel. Hopper access can automate transfers and a comparator reads its inventory.

§6COMMON USES§r
Potion brewing lines and inventory-status indicators.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
The order of ingredients matters. A powered redstone line is not a direct brewing start button.

entries.title: Lectern
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Holds a readable book. Turning pages produces a redstone pulse, and a comparator reads a signal based on the current page position.

§6COMMON USES§r
Page-selected puzzles and secret doors.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
This custom guide is a menu item, not a vanilla written book, so it cannot be placed on a lectern. Use a normal written book for a lectern circuit.

entries.title: Chiseled bookshelf
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Stores six books. A comparator reports the most recently interacted-with slot, not how many books the shelf holds.

§6COMMON USES§r
Secret book switches and slot-selection puzzles.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
An ordinary bookshelf does not have this redstone behavior.

entries.title: Shelf
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Displays three item stacks. Redstone power changes its interaction so a player can exchange a section of their hotbar with the shelf. Adjacent powered shelves can work together.

§6COMMON USES§r
Quick tool-loadout swapping and equipment stations.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Power prepares the swapping interaction; it does not automatically exchange your inventory when you walk past.

entries.title: Cauldron
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A comparator can read its fill state. Bedrock supports more cauldron contents than Java, so use the correct content for your design.

§6COMMON USES§r
Rain or liquid-level sensing and decorative analog controls.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Test the output with a short dust line after changing its contents.

entries.title: Composter
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Organic items can increase its compost level and eventually produce bone meal. A comparator reads the current level.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic composters and excess-crop recycling.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Load compostable items with a hopper above and collect bone meal below. Not every accepted item has the same composting chance.

entries.title: Cake
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A comparator can read how much cake remains. Eating slices changes the output.

§6COMMON USES§r
Edible combination controls and compact adjustable signal sources.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
The setting is consumed when you eat it. Plan to replace the cake when it runs out.

entries.title: Item frame and glow item frame
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A comparator can read an inserted item's rotation through the full solid block behind the frame. Rotating the item changes the signal.

§6COMMON USES§r
Combination locks and selectable analog settings.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A glow item frame makes the display easier to see; it is not itself a light-emitting power source.

entries.title: Jukebox
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Plays inserted music discs. A comparator can distinguish discs using their output strengths, making disc choice useful as an input.

§6COMMON USES§r
Music-controlled puzzles and disc selectors.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Disc signal behavior is not the same as ordinary inventory fullness. Check the exact disc in your Bedrock build.

entries.title: Beehive and bee nest
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A comparator reads the honey level. Full honey indicates that the block is ready to harvest.

§6COMMON USES§r
Automatic honey-bottle or honeycomb collection.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A dispenser with the appropriate harvesting item can automate collection. Keep your bees safe when testing harvesting behavior.

entries.title: Copper golem statue
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
A fully oxidized copper golem can become a statue. Its pose can be changed by interaction and read with a comparator.

§6COMMON USES§r
Decorative combination controls and pose-selection puzzles.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A statue is a block, not an active sorting golem. Waxing and scraping affect its oxidation state.

entries.title: Respawn anchor
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Stores glowstone charges for Nether respawning. A comparator can read its charge level.

§6COMMON USES§r
Charge-status indicators for Nether bases.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Using an anchor in the wrong dimension can cause an explosion. It is not a safe decorative switch in an Overworld house.

entries.title: Rail
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Carries minecarts. Power can influence the selected direction at a suitable rail junction, but ordinary rails do not accelerate a cart by themselves.

§6COMMON USES§r
Rail routes, junctions, and hopper-minecart collection systems.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Check junction direction with an empty cart before you send valuable cargo through it.

entries.title: Powered rail
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Accelerates minecarts when powered and brakes them when unpowered.

§6COMMON USES§r
Stations, launchers, hills, and maintaining speed along a route.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
A stationary cart needs a useful launch direction, such as a slope or a solid block behind an end rail.

entries.title: Detector rail
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Emits power when a minecart passes over or rests on it. Comparator readings can inspect supported container minecarts on the rail.

§6COMMON USES§r
Arrival sensors, traffic signals, and unloading stations.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
This is a sensor, not an accelerator.

entries.title: Activator rail
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
When powered, it triggers the special behavior of a compatible minecart: ejecting riders, priming TNT carts, or changing hopper-cart collection.

§6COMMON USES§r
Passenger unloading and controlling specialized minecarts.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
It is not a powered rail. Do not use it as a substitute for track acceleration.

entries.title: Minecart with hopper
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Collects items along its route, including through a full block above it, and can be emptied into a hopper beneath the track.

§6COMMON USES§r
Collecting drops under farm soil and fast moving pickup systems.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Keep a stationary collection cart from rolling away. A powered activator rail disables its pickup until re-enabled by an unpowered activator rail.

entries.title: Minecart with chest
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Moves a storage inventory along rails. Hoppers can load or unload it when positioned correctly, and a comparator on a detector rail can read it.

§6COMMON USES§r
Cargo transport and minecart-based storage delivery.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Stop the cart long enough to transfer the intended load.

entries.title: Minecart with TNT
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Carries an explosive payload. A powered activator rail can prime it; impacts and other conditions can also make it dangerous.

§6COMMON USES§r
Specialized demolition and controlled minigames in disposable worlds.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Do not send one through a valuable transport system.

entries.title: Command block
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Runs a configured command. Impulse blocks run once when triggered; repeating blocks run repeatedly while enabled; chain blocks follow a command chain.

§6COMMON USES§r
Adventure maps, minigames, and administrator-controlled automation.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Command blocks are not survival-craftable. They require the appropriate commands and permissions. This guide itself needs no command blocks.

entries.title: Sculk shrieker
pages:
§6HOW IT WORKS§r
Responds to relevant player activity and sculk-sensor activation. Naturally generated shriekers can contribute to summoning a Warden.

§6COMMON USES§r
Adventure-map sound effects and sculk-themed mechanisms.

§eTRY THIS / TIP§r
Player-placed shriekers do not summon Wardens. This is not a general replacement for a redstone power source or ordinary alarm lamp.

entries.title: 1. Automatic night lights
pages:
§6MATERIALS§r
1 daylight detector; 1 repeater; 1 redstone lamp; 4 redstone dust; full solid support blocks.

§6BUILD§r
1. Make a flat row of support blocks outside under open sky.
2. On the row place: detector > dust > dust > dust > dust > repeater > lamp.
3. Point the repeater toward the lamp.
4. Use the detector until it is in inverted (night) mode.

§6RESULT§r
A nonzero signal at the repeater becomes full strength and lights the lamp. As the sky darkens, the lamp switches on without another button press.

§6TEST AND IMPROVE§r
Wait for night and then daylight. Weather and sky exposure affect the switching threshold, so test it where it will actually be used.

Add more lamps after the repeater, with dust and extra repeaters as needed. Keep each wire run short enough to retain a positive signal.

§6TROUBLESHOOT§r
Always on in daytime? Check that the detector is inverted.
Never on? Check the repeater direction and the dust path.
Unpredictable threshold? Remove the roof above the detector and test in clear weather.

§eThis uses a redstone lamp, not a copper bulb: a bulb toggles state rather than directly following day/night power.

entries.title: 2. Button-operated iron door
pages:
§6MATERIALS§r
1 iron door; 2 wooden buttons; 1 full solid block, plus your wall and floor.

§6BUILD§r
1. Place the iron door in an opening on a solid floor.
2. Put a full stone block immediately beside the LOWER half of the door, at the same height as that half.
3. Attach one wooden button to the outside-facing side of this stone block.
4. Attach the second button to its inside-facing side.
5. Press either button. The powered stone block opens the adjacent door.

§6RESULT§r
The door opens briefly and then closes. Both sides have a way through.

§6TEST AND IMPROVE§r
Try the outside button, walk through, and test the inside button. Do this before sealing the rest of the room.

Wooden buttons give about 1.5 seconds to enter under normal game speed. A lever can hold the door open instead.

§6OPTIONAL AUTOMATIC EXIT§r
A stone pressure plate immediately beside the lower half of the door can act as an inside exit trigger. Remember that mobs can activate stone plates too.

§6TROUBLESHOOT§r
The button must be attached to the full block beside the lower door half, not to a remote wall. Glass is not a substitute for the conducting stone block.

entries.title: 3. Automatic sugar cane harvester
pages:
§6MATERIALS§r
1 dirt; 1 sugar cane; water beside the dirt; 1 piston; 1 observer; 1 redstone dust; 1 full solid wiring block; glass for an enclosure.

§6BUILD ONE CELL§r
1. Plant sugar cane on dirt with water directly beside the dirt.
2. Put a piston behind the cane, facing the space where the SECOND cane block will grow. Leave the bottom cane untouched.
3. Place an observer directly on top of the piston. Its face watches the THIRD cane position; its red dot faces away from the cane.
4. Put a full solid block directly behind the piston. Put dust on top of that block. The observer's red dot now points into this dust.
5. Enclose the sides with glass, leaving the growth spaces clear.

§6WHAT HAPPENS§r
When the third cane grows, the observer powers the dust behind it. The block below that dust powers the adjacent piston. The piston breaks the upper cane, leaving the bottom to regrow.

§6AUTOMATIC COLLECTION§r
Place a stationary hopper minecart on a rail directly beneath the dirt supporting the cane. Put a hopper below the rail, aimed into a chest. The cart collects drops through the dirt; the hopper empties the cart. Contain the rail so the cart cannot roll away.

§6TEST§r
Manually place cane until it is three high. Check that only the upper section breaks and that the base survives. Then test collection before duplicating the cell.

§eThis is a sugar cane design. Do not use it as an automatic wheat-replanting tutorial.
